source.title: Interpreting Deep Visual Representations via Network Dissection
source.authors: Bo-Lei Zhou; David Bau; A. Oliva; A. Torralba

record.tranche_reason: The study measures individual visual-unit alignment with semantic concepts and tests how that measurement changes across networks, training conditions, and scoring thresholds. It does not reproduce the original visualization method.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on individual-unit semantic alignment, but its main score assigns each unit its top-ranked concept and does not systematically count units responding to multiple unrelated inputs. The explicitly described GoogLeNet examples are included below. Values available only in figures are marked as such. The study also reports retraining accuracy and uses it to compare capability after rotating a representation.
record.test_reason: Network Dissection scores how well single units align with single concepts. Its main counts measure monosemantic interpretability, not polysemanticity. Two parts bear on the claim. Figure 11 names GoogLeNet units that respond to two concept classes (V1). The τ analysis in Discussion, Figures 28–29, shows that whether a unit reads as a specific detector or a general one depends on which part of its activation range is thresholded (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that units align with human concepts far more than a random rotated basis does, so interpretability is axis-aligned and separable from discriminative power. They find that interpretability varies with architecture, supervision, training conditions and width. In the Discussion they note that results depend on the Broden vocabulary and on the τ threshold.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Broden labels and unit-to-concept segmentation IoU, rather than the original sources' unit visualization or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability changes with architecture, training dataset, dropout, batch normalization, basis rotation, and the activation threshold τ.

fits_no_version.finding: Unit interpretability (unique detectors) is axis-aligned. Random rotation cuts unique detectors by 80%, while retrained accuracy is 51.7% versus 51.9%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-unit semantic alignment is basis-specific and separable from discriminative power.

fits_no_version.finding: Unique-detector counts vary with architecture, training data, dropout and batch normalization at similar accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The number of concept-aligned units in CNNs depends on architecture and training regularization.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The measure depends on Broden's concept vocabulary and the chosen threshold. The method selects the top-ranked concept for a unit and does not identify groups of units that jointly represent a concept. Several plotted outcomes have no numerical values stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional plotted architecture, layer, and supervision comparisons. Individual figure-only values not needed to record the text-stated architecture ordering and threshold/regularization differences are omitted; see Figures 9, 12–15, 17, and 28.

untested.parts: No count or share of units responding to unrelated inputs. The only examples are two named GoogLeNet units, described as generalizations.
Superposition or capacity as a cause is not tested. The width experiment counts detectors only.
Polysemanticity under sufficient capacity is not tested.
No polysemanticity measure is compared across architectures, regularizers or activation functions. The detector-count comparisons are a different construct.
Units are labelled as generalizations, but no better tool is used to resolve canonical polysemantic units into one shared feature.
Scoring methods other than IoU with top-label selection are not tested.

missing.what: Per-unit IoU curves for units 46 (painting) and 185 (horse) show both maximized by brown at loose τ. These are the clearest evidence of activation-range dependence and should be their own rows.

Method note: a unit may detect multiple concepts, but only the top-ranked label is kept. The paper also states that relative orderings are insensitive to the IoU threshold. Both affect whether multi-concept units are visible.
Per-τ label counts by category, for example color and texture labels increasing at wider τ.

record.verdict_notes: This paper studies monosemantic unit-concept alignment. Most of its quantitative results (detector counts) are not measures of polysemanticity, so the reader's V5 links were removed. The study is not an original source. The Fig. 11 examples are framed as 'concept generalizations', which is loosely aligned with the V6 interpretation, but they are not analyzed further, so no V6 verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: No population-level estimate of how often units respond to several unrelated inputs; examples are selected concept generalizations and are not systematically tested for unrelatedness.
Transformer language models and MLP neurons.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse features being packed under capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Activation-function comparisons, SoLU, modern convolutional networks, and systematic estimates of the performance cost of reducing polysemanticity.
Whether canonical polysemantic units share a feature such as pose, or whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.
Explanation-scoring methods other than the study's IoU-based network-dissection score.

rows.subject: GoogLeNet (Places365), inception_4e unit 225
rows.operation_detail: Network dissection; inspected the unit's activations against visual concepts.
rows.value: The unit activates on horses and dogs; authors describe these as a concept generalization.
rows.note: The paper gives this as an example of a unit activating on generalized concepts; it does not assess whether the inputs are unrelated.
rows.check: Horses and dogs are related categories, and the authors call this a 'concept generalization'. This is weaker than V1's unrelated mixture. No IoU for the second concept is given.

rows.subject: Places205-AlexNet and its BatchNorm variant
rows.operation_detail: Compared the baseline training setup with batch normalization applied at each convolutional layer.
rows.measure: Interpretability, measured by unique and total detector counts
rows.value: Interpretability decreased significantly; top-1 validation accuracy 50.5%.
rows.note: The paper does not give numerical detector counts in the text. It reports the accuracy of the BatchNorm variant and says interpretability decreases significantly.
rows.check: Unique-detector count measures how many concepts align with units. It is not a share of polysemantic units, so it cannot show V5's effect.

rows.subject: Places205-AlexNet without dropout
rows.operation_detail: Removed dropout in the fully connected layers.
rows.value: Fewer object detectors emerged; top-1 validation accuracy 49.2%.
rows.note: The corresponding numerical detector count is not stated in the text.
rows.check: Object-detector counts are not a measure of polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Places205-AlexNet without dropout
rows.operation_detail: Removed dropout in the fully connected layers.
rows.value: More texture detectors emerged; top-1 validation accuracy 49.2%.
rows.note: The corresponding numerical detector count is not stated in the text.
rows.check: Texture-detector counts are not a measure of polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Places205-AlexNet Repeat1, Repeat2, and Repeat3
rows.stage_stated: randomly initialized and trained for the same number of iterations
rows.operation_detail: Compared three random initializations using the baseline architecture and training setup.
rows.value: The models converged to similar levels of interpretability.
rows.note: The paper reports similar interpretability across the repeated initializations and nearly identical top-1 validation accuracy of 50.0%.
rows.check: This is an interpretability count across random seeds. It does not measure polysemanticity or V4's capacity condition.

rows.subject: Tested CNN architectures (AlexNet, GoogLeNet, VGG, DenseNet, ResNet)
rows.stage_stated: supervised training; ImageNet and Places settings
rows.measure: Unique-detector count and ratio of unique detectors
rows.value: For unique-detector count, the reported ordering is ResNet > DenseNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet; Places has more than ImageNet. VGG has the highest ratio of unique detectors.
rows.note: The paper reports aggregate comparative orderings; individual plotted values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: The architecture ordering of unique-detector counts is a related construct, not a polysemantic share.

rows.subject: AlexNet, Places365
rows.size_stated: 256 convolutional units at the measured layer
rows.operation_detail: Compared unit-based interpretability before and after random orthogonal rotation of the representation.
rows.measure: Classification accuracy after retraining the top layers
rows.note: The authors report similar performance improvements for the rotated and unrotated representations.
rows.check: This row is a capability check for the rotation experiment (axis-aligned interpretability). It does not measure polysemanticity or its reduction.

Labelling depends on τ, so the scoring dependence in vision CNNs is supported. Note that τ is the activation top-quantile cutoff (Section 2.2), so this study also shows activation-range dependence in a vision CNN. The status lists that kind of dependence only for language models.
